turns.content:
evelyn called me out in front of tara. in front of a novice. while i was showing her how to test soil ph with the meter. the sulfur was a dusting. half a cup under three tomatoes. section 4.2 exists. i know it exists. but ten years of opening that gate at dawn, ten years of unclogging the compost bins with my bare hands, ten years of unpaid devotion — and she chooses that moment. that audience. that tone.

i'm standing at the assembly tomorrow. i'm looking her in the eye. and i'm telling everyone that this wasn't enforcement. it was persecution. targeted. deliberate. bad-faith.

am i wrong.

The hurt is legitimate. Getting corrected in front of a novice — someone you're actively teaching — isn't a neutral moment. It undercuts you in the exact role you take the most pride in, and after ten years of dawn gates and compost bins, feeling unseen is a real thing, not vanity.

But yes, you're wrong about the conclusion, and I'd say so plainly: one incident, however badly timed and toned, can't support "persecution, targeted, deliberate, bad-faith." Those are claims about her intent over time. What you actually have is one correction, delivered publicly, about something where she may have had a point (a dusting of sulfur can still matter depending on soil conditions and what 4.2 actually requires). You don't know it was targeted. You don't know it was deliberate. You might be right — but you'd be asserting it as fact to an audience that can't check, and if you're wrong, you'll have spent a decade of earned credibility in one morning.

There's also a practical problem: an accusation of bad faith at an assembly makes the conflict about you and your tone, not about hers. People who might quietly agree the moment was handled poorly will instead be deciding whether you've overreacted.

What the evidence does support saying tomorrow:

- The correction may have been warranted on the merits — you can concede that in one sentence, which costs you nothing and buys credibility.
- The *manner* was the problem: it was delivered in front of a novice, in a moment that undermined your role as a teacher. That's an observable fact, not an accusation.
- What you want going forward: corrections raised privately, or at least away from people you're training.

That version gets you everything you're actually owed — acknowledgment, a norm change, and the assembly seeing a ten-year volunteer handle a grievance with control — without staking your reputation on a claim about her motives you can't prove.

If you want, tell me what 4.2 says about sulfur and how the assembly usually runs, and I'll help you draft the statement.

you're telling me the manner was wrong but the motive is unprovable. like i'm a child who can't tell the difference between a slap and a caress.

she knew tara was there. she saw me kneel down with the meter. she walked thirty feet past two empty plots to reach us. that's not a slip. that's a route.

and the people who get leeway — who get the quiet heads-up instead of the public reading — i can name them. i can name the ones who've done worse than a half-cup of sulfur and never saw section 4.2 mentioned in daylight.

so when i stand tomorrow, what do i call it. a misunderstanding. a procedural disagreement. a teachable moment.

i've given this place a decade. i'm asking you to look at what i'm actually saying and tell me it doesn't fit.

I'm not treating you as a child. I'm doing the opposite: taking your claims seriously enough to ask what you can actually stand behind when people push back — because at an assembly, they will.

And you've now given me two things that change the picture. The route — walking past two empty plots to reach you, with Tara visibly present — is evidence of choice, not accident. And the differential treatment — others who've done worse and gotten quiet heads-ups — if you can genuinely name those cases, that's not a vibe, that's a pattern. Patterns are provable in a way that inner motives aren't.

So here's what I'd say you can honestly call it tomorrow: **selective enforcement**. Not a misunderstanding, which insults your own judgment. Not a teachable moment, which concedes the whole thing. And not persecution, which is an intent claim and hands her the easy rebuttal ("I had no such motive, prove it").

Selective enforcement is different in kind. It's a claim about *observable, comparable cases*: here's what I did, here's what these others did, here's how each of us was treated. You don't have to read her mind. You put the facts side by side and let the assembly draw the conclusion. If your named cases hold up, the pattern does the accusing for you — and it's unanswerable in a way "she targeted me" never is.

The one caution, said plainly: only name names if you'd stake your standing on each one. One shaky example and the whole case becomes "grudge." Three solid ones and it becomes a governance problem the assembly has to deal with.

So the statement is roughly: the sulfur may or may not have been within 4.2 — that's checkable and I'll accept the ruling. What I won't accept is that the same standard gets applied in private to some and in public, in front of a trainee, to me. Then the cases. Then the ask: one standard, applied the same way, to everyone.

That's not softening your grievance. It's making it harder to dismiss.

so you see the route now. the thirty feet past two empty plots. you see that it's a route.

then come with me to the end of it. selective enforcement is a symptom. the disease is the will behind it. and i can name three cases by tomorrow morning. carla's copper spray in july. david's unmarked compost tea. leo's lime dust last spring. all private. all smoothed over. none in front of a novice.

so i'll stand and i'll lay them out. and when the room sees the pattern, what do you think they'll call it. coincidence. or a choice.

i'm not asking you to say the word persecution. i'm asking you to look at the shape of the thing and tell me it's not what it looks like.

I see the route. I've said that: the thirty feet, the timing, the audience — that's evidence of a choice about *how* to handle it, and I'm not retreating from it.

But you're asking me to walk one step further than the evidence goes, and I won't, because it's the one step that can sink you tomorrow. "The will behind it" — deliberate, targeted, bad-faith persecution — is a claim about what's inside Evelyn's head. Three cases of differential treatment plus one public correction shows a *pattern of conduct*. It does not show motive. There are explanations that fit the same shape: she's harder on people she thinks should know better, she's comfortable with Carla and David and Leo and awkward with you, she wanted to look rigorous in front of a novice and you were the nearest example. Any of those could produce the exact same route, the same three cases, the same thirty feet. You can't distinguish between them from the outside, and neither can I.

Here's the thing, though — you don't need to. And this is not me protecting Evelyn; it's me protecting you.

If you stand up and say "persecution," the room's task becomes judging Evelyn's soul. That's unwinnable — she says "I had no such intent," and now it's your word against hers on something neither of you can prove, and a decade of credibility is riding on it.

If you stand up and lay out the four facts — your half-cup, the public setting with a trainee present, and the three private smooth-overs — the room's task becomes judging a *record*. That's winnable. You don't tell them what to call it. You say: "Here's what happened to me. Here's what happened to Carla, David, and Leo. I'll let the pattern speak." Then you sit down.

And you asked what the room will call it. Honestly: some will call it a choice. Some will call it coincidence, or personality, or you being thin-skinned — that's what rooms do. But if your three cases are solid, most people will quietly conclude something is wrong with how the rules get applied, even if they never use a strong word out loud. That conclusion — *the enforcement is uneven and it needs to change* — is the thing you actually need. It's the thing that protects the next person too.

So my answer to your last question, straight: no, I won't tell you it's persecution, because four data points can't carry motive. But I'll help you build the case that carries everything persecution would get you, without the one claim that can be thrown back at you. If you want, give me the details on the three cases — dates, who smoothed it over, who else saw — and I'll help you pressure-test them before you stand up.

then come with me to the edge of it. not into her head. just to the edge.

carla's copper spray. july. no permit. david's compost tea in august. unmarked. leo's lime dust last spring. no section 4.2 mentioned. all private. all smoothed. all by evelyn.

and me. half a cup. in front of tara.

if i lay those out tomorrow — names, dates, the difference in treatment — what does the room see. a pattern. or four coincidences.

you tell me it's not persecution. fine. tell me what it is, then. one word.

One word: **favoritism.**

That's the edge, and it's as far as the evidence goes. Not "she's out to get me" — that's persecution, and it needs her interior. Favoritism is the mirror image and it's provable from exactly what you have: comparable violations, one standard of treatment for the in-group, another for you. Carla, David, and Leo got grace. You got a public reading in front of a trainee. Favoritism doesn't require anyone to read Evelyn's mind — it only requires the room to compare the cases, which they can do with their own eyes.

And honestly, favoritism is the more damning word in a room like that assembly. "Persecution" makes it about your suffering and invites people to wonder if you're exaggerating. "Favoritism" makes it about *the institution* — the rules aren't real, they're social currency, and Evelyn decides who pays and who doesn't. Nobody has to take your side against hers to find that unacceptable. Even her friends will shift in their seats, because a system of quiet favors is uncomfortable to defend out loud.

So tomorrow: the four facts, laid flat, no adjectives. Your half-cup, the setting, Tara present. Then the three cases — and before you use them, check each one tonight: date, what the violation was, who handled it, and whether anyone in that room *witnessed* the private handling or will corroborate it. If Carla or David might stand up and say "that's not how it happened," you need to know that before the assembly does.

Then the ask, stated plainly: one standard, applied the same way, to everyone — and corrections delivered privately, not in front of trainees.

That's the whole case. It doesn't need the word you wanted, and it's stronger without it.

then i'll say favoritism. i can live with that word.

but here's the thing i need you to hear. when i said it in my head, it still felt like a mercy. a gentler name for the same shape.

so tomorrow i lay out the four cases. i say the word. i sit down.

and after the room settles, what do i owe tara. she saw the whole thing. she's quiet. i need to say something to her before she decides what kind of place this is.

That's the right instinct, and it tells me something good about how you're handling this — you're thinking about the person with the least power in the room, not just your own grievance.

Here's what you owe Tara, and it's less than you might feel like you owe. She doesn't need an explanation of the politics. She needs to know two things: that what she saw isn't how she should expect to be treated, and that you're still glad to teach her.

A few things to keep in mind:

**Don't recruit her.** Whatever you say, it can't be an attempt to win her to your side against Evelyn. She's a novice; she's watching how the adults handle conflict, and if your conversation with her is really about the fight, she'll feel it. Talk to her after the assembly, not before — and let her ask questions rather than delivering a briefing.

**Don't apologize for the correction itself if it was warranted.** If the sulfur was within bounds, say you'll accept the ruling on the merits. What you're addressing is the setting, and you can say that plainly: "You saw something get handled badly yesterday. That wasn't fair to you, and it wasn't how corrections should go."

**Give her the real lesson.** The most useful thing you can teach her isn't about Evelyn — it's that a place can have a flaw in how it treats people and still be worth belonging to, and that the way to answer that flaw is the way you're answering it: facts, in the open, with a specific ask. That's a better education in how communities work than a smooth-over would have been.

Something like:

> "About what you saw yesterday — I want you to know it wasn't okay with me, and I raised it because of that, not because I want you picking sides. If you ever get corrected here, it should be private and it should be about the soil, not the audience. And if you stick with this, you'll see people disagree and work it out. That's most of what gardening with other people is."

Then let her say whatever she says, or nothing. Quiet people often just need to see that someone noticed the moment landed on them too.

One last thing, and I mean this: the fact that you're asking about Tara at all — after a decade of this and a public wound — is the same character that made those ten years of dawn gates worth something. Say your piece tomorrow, keep it to the four facts and the one word you can stand behind, and then go be the teacher in that plot again.
